column1: What is the 'multimodal advantage' formally defined as, in information-theoretic terms?
column2: The gap I(Y; X₁,...,Xₙ) − max_i I(Y; Xᵢ): the additional mutual information about target Y captured by the joint set of modalities versus the single best modality alone.

column1: Why does the data-processing inequality guarantee that a joint conditional P(Y|X_text, X_image,...) is never less informative than any marginal P(Y|Xᵢ)?
column2: Because no transformation of a subset of inputs can recover information discarded by ignoring other inputs; this is a theorem, so I(Y; X₁,...,Xₙ) ≥ I(Y; Xᵢ) for any single modality i.

column1: What are the three structural invariants that govern every multimodal architecture regardless of implementation?
column2: Semantic alignment (same real-world event maps to nearby embeddings across modalities), temporal coherence (co-occurring events aligned in time before fusion), and modality-agnostic task representation (final task head not committed to any single modality's structure).

column1: Why do late-fusion architectures that concatenate independent CLS tokens underperform cross-modal attention architectures?
column2: Concatenation preserves modality identity in the activation geometry, which impedes the model's ability to learn cross-modal correlations before the task head.

column1: What makes Gemini's architecture 'natively multimodal' rather than a pipeline-based approach like LLaVA?
column2: Gemini is trained from scratch on interleaved text, image, audio, and video sequences in a single shared token embedding space, so attention operates across all modality tokens at every layer — there is no separate 'tower' whose output is projected afterward into the text space.

column1: How are variable-resolution images handled in Gemini's token encoding, and why does this matter?
column2: Via dynamic patch counts rather than fixed resizing — the number of image tokens scales with image size/tiling instead of forcing all images into one fixed resolution, preserving detail and directly affecting token budget.

column1: In the LLaVA-style architecture, what is the 'projection gap' and how does Gemini's design eliminate it?
column2: The projection gap is the mismatch between a separate vision encoder's (e.g., CLIP ViT) embedding dimension and the LLM's embedding dimension, bridged via a projection MLP. Gemini eliminates this by training all modalities from scratch into one shared tokenizer/embedding space, at the cost of requiring massive cross-modal pretraining data.

column1: What are the three governing invariants for performance optimization of multimodal API systems?
column2: Token Budget (computational invariant — total tokens drive FLOPs, cost, and context limits), Memory Bandwidth (memory invariant — KV-cache size for long contexts), and Network I/O (communication invariant — large media payload upload latency).

column1: Approximately how many tokens does Gemini 1.5+ use to encode a 768×768 image tile, and what consequence does this have?
column2: Roughly 258 tokens per tile; since each image/video frame consumes many tokens, this directly inflates the token budget, FLOPs cost, and risk of hitting the context window limit.

column1: Why does prefill cost in a 1M-token Gemini context window scale super-linearly with sequence length?
column2: Because the transformer's self-attention mechanism has quadratic computational complexity in sequence length, so doubling tokens more than doubles the attention compute cost.

column1: What production feature should be used instead of resending the same large media payload on every conversational turn, and why?
column2: Context caching (a first-class Gemini 1.5+ API feature) — it avoids unnecessary KV-cache re-hydration and redundant network/compute cost from re-processing the same large media repeatedly.

column1: In the Gemini API request lifecycle, what is the difference between the input safety filter and the output safety filter, and can either be fully disabled in production?
column2: The input filter runs before inference to block harmful prompts at the category level; the output filter runs on generated tokens applying the same category thresholds. Both are configurable via `safety_settings` but cannot be fully disabled on production models.
